body.q: A business owner takes goods from the business inventory for personal use and does not record the transaction. Which accounting concept has been ignored?
body.why: The business entity concept requires the owner's personal transactions to be kept separate from those of the business, so goods taken must be recorded as drawings.

body.q: A trader values closing inventory at cost price rather than at the higher selling price. Which accounting concept is being applied?
body.why: Prudence means profits and assets should not be overstated, so inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value.

body.q: A business has always used the reducing balance method to depreciate its vehicles. This year it uses the straight-line method purely to show a higher profit. Which concept has been broken?
body.why: Consistency requires the same accounting methods to be used from one period to the next so that results can be compared.

o: The skill and loyalty of its employees
body.q: Which of the following could NOT be recorded in the accounts of a business because of the money measurement concept?
body.why: Money measurement means only items that can be expressed in monetary terms are recorded, and the quality of staff cannot be given a reliable money value.

body.q: A business buys a machine for $20 000. A year later a similar machine costs $24 000. The machine remains in the accounts at $20 000 less depreciation. Which concept is being applied?
body.why: Historic cost means assets are recorded at the price originally paid rather than at their current market value.

body.q: A business records a sale when the goods are delivered and the invoice is sent to the customer, even though payment is received the following month. Which concept does this show?
body.why: Realisation states that revenue is recognised when goods or services are supplied, not when the cash is received.

body.q: A business pays $1 200 in December for insurance covering the following year. Which concept requires the expense to be shown in the following year's income statement?
body.why: The matching concept requires expenses to be recorded in the same period as the revenue they helped to earn, regardless of when they were paid.

body.q: A business buys a stapler for $4 and records it as an expense rather than as a non-current asset. Which concept justifies this treatment?
body.why: Materiality allows insignificant items to be treated in the simplest way, as the amount is too small to affect decisions.

body.q: The accountant of a business prepares the financial statements assuming that the business will continue to trade for the foreseeable future. Which concept is being applied?
body.why: The going concern concept assumes the business will continue to operate, so assets are not valued as if they were about to be sold off.

body.q: A business purchases a computer on credit. It records an increase in non-current assets and an increase in payables. Which concept does this illustrate?
body.why: The dual aspect concept states that every transaction has two effects on the accounts, so each debit entry has a matching credit entry.

body.q: At the year end, a business has paid $1 200 for insurance covering 12 months from 1 October. The financial year ends on 31 December. What is the amount of prepaid insurance at 31 December?
body.why: Nine of the twelve months (January to September) fall in the next year, so 9/12 × $1 200 = $900 is prepaid.

body.q: A business has accrued expenses of $450 for electricity at the year end. How is this shown in the statement of financial position?
body.why: Accrued expenses are amounts owed at the year end and are therefore current liabilities.

body.q: Rent paid during the year was $6 000. Rent prepaid at the end of the year was $500. What is the rent expense shown in the income statement?
body.why: Prepaid rent relates to the next year, so it is deducted: $6 000 - $500 = $5 500.

body.q: A business has a trade receivables balance of $20 000 and wants to create a allowance for doubtful debts of 5%. There was no previous allowance. What is the entry in the income statement?
body.why: 5% × $20 000 = $1 000, and creating a new allowance is recorded as an expense.

o: Reduction in expenses (or increase in profit) of $150
body.q: The allowance for doubtful debts was $800 at the start of the year. At the end of the year it is calculated as $650. How is the change treated in the income statement?
body.why: The allowance has decreased by $150, so too much was previously charged and the difference increases profit.

body.q: A machine cost $40 000 and is depreciated at 20% per year using the reducing balance method. What is the depreciation charge for the second year?
body.why: Year 1 is $8 000, leaving a net book value of $32 000, and 20% of $32 000 = $6 400.

body.q: A vehicle cost $25 000 and has an expected residual value of $5 000 after 5 years. What is the annual depreciation charge using the straight-line method?
body.why: Straight-line depreciation is (cost - residual value) ÷ useful life = $20 000 ÷ 5 = $4 000.

body.q: Which of the following is an example of income received in advance at the year end?
body.why: Income received in advance is cash received during the year that relates to a future period, such as commission for next year.

body.q: A business has wages of $18 000 paid during the year. At the year end, $1 500 of wages is owing. What is the wages expense for the year?
body.why: Owing wages are added to the amount paid: $18 000 + $1 500 = $19 500.

body.q: Why does a business make adjustments for accruals and prepayments before preparing its final accounts?
body.why: Adjustments apply the matching concept so that income and expenses are recorded in the period they relate to, regardless of when cash is paid or received.

o: A cheque paid to a supplier of $450 has not yet been presented to the bank
A cheque received from a customer of $450 has been recorded in the cash book but not yet paid into the bank
Bank charges of $450 appear on the bank statement but not in the cash book
A direct debit of $450 appears on the bank statement but not in the cash book
body.q: A business's cash book shows a bank balance of $4,200 debit. The bank statement shows a balance of $4,650. Which of the following could explain the difference?
body.why: An unpresented cheque reduces the cash book but not yet the bank statement, so the statement balance is higher than the cash book balance.

o: Bank charges shown on the bank statement
A cheque paid in that the bank has not yet processed
body.q: Which of the following items would require an entry in the cash book when preparing a bank reconciliation?
body.why: Bank charges appear on the statement but not in the cash book, so the cash book must be updated; the other items are timing differences that only affect the reconciliation statement.

body.q: On 31 May, a business's cash book shows a bank balance of $2,800 debit. The bank statement shows a credit of $3,000 for a customer's direct transfer that is not yet in the cash book. What is the updated cash book balance?
body.why: Adding the unrecorded $3,000 receipt to the $2,800 debit balance gives $5,800.

o: Credit the bank column in the cash book
Debit the bank column in the cash book
Make no entry until the customer pays again
body.q: A cheque received from a customer was paid into the bank but was later returned by the bank marked 'refer to drawer'. How should the business record this in its cash book?
body.why: A dishonoured cheque means the money never arrived, so the earlier debit in the bank column is reversed by a credit.

o: To check that the cash book and the bank statement agree, and to find any errors or omissions
To calculate the profit for the year
To show the total amount owed to suppliers
To record all cash sales made during the month
body.q: Which of the following is the main purpose of preparing a bank reconciliation statement?
body.why: A bank reconciliation compares the cash book with the bank statement to explain differences and detect errors.

body.q: A business has an overdraft. The cash book shows a bank balance of $(1,500) overdrawn. Unpresented cheques total $400 and outstanding lodgements total $900. What balance should the bank statement show?
body.why: Starting from the cash book balance of -1,500, add back unpresented cheques (+400) to get -1,100 and then deduct outstanding lodgements (-900) to get -2,000.

o: Interest received by the bank not recorded in the cash book
A standing order received by the bank not yet in the cash book
body.q: Which of the following would cause the bank statement balance to be lower than the cash book balance (both in credit)?
body.why: Outstanding lodgements are recorded in the cash book but not yet credited by the bank, so the statement shows a lower balance.

o: No entry is needed because the bank has already recorded it
body.q: A business receives its bank statement showing a direct debit of $120 for insurance that has not been entered in the cash book. What entry should be made in the cash book?
body.why: A payment out of the bank account is recorded as a credit in the bank column of the cash book.

body.q: The cash book shows a bank balance of $3,500 debit. Bank interest of $50 charged and a standing order of $200 paid are on the statement but not in the cash book. What is the corrected cash book balance?
body.why: Both items are payments, so deduct them: 3,500 - 50 - 200 = 3,250.

o: A cheque issued by the business that has not yet been paid by the bank
A cheque received from a customer that has not yet been banked
A cheque returned by the bank because the customer has insufficient funds
A cheque that the bank has cleared but the business has not recorded
body.q: Which of the following describes an unpresented cheque?
body.why: An unpresented cheque is one the business has written and recorded but which the payee has not yet cashed, so it has not appeared on the bank statement.

body.q: Which book of original entry is used to record credit sales of goods to customers?
body.why: The sales journal records credit sales, taken from invoices issued to customers.

body.q: A business returns goods bought on credit to a supplier. Which document is the source for entering this in the purchases returns journal?
body.why: The supplier sends a credit note to confirm the reduction in the amount owed, and this is used to record the return.

o: Purchase of office furniture on credit
Return of goods by a customer
body.q: Which transaction would be recorded in the general journal?
body.why: Purchases of non-current assets on credit are not goods for resale, so they are recorded in the general journal rather than the purchases journal.

o: Goods sold on credit to J. Singh
body.q: Which of the following is recorded in the cash book?
body.why: The cash book records all receipts and payments of cash and bank, including cheques paid.

body.q: A trader buys goods for resale on credit from K. Rao for $800. In which book of original entry is this first recorded?
body.why: Credit purchases of goods for resale are entered in the purchases journal from the supplier's invoice.

body.q: What is the main source document for entries in the sales returns journal?
body.why: When a customer returns goods, the business issues a credit note, which is used to make the entry.

o: Recording the purchase of non-current assets
body.q: Which entry is a purpose of the petty cash book?
body.why: The petty cash book records small, low-value expenses such as postage and stationery.

body.q: In a three-column cash book, what do the three columns on each side represent?
body.why: A three-column cash book has columns for discount, cash and bank on both the debit and credit sides.

o: To record transactions in date order before posting to the ledger
To prepare the final statement of financial position directly
To calculate the profit for the year
To replace the need for a trial balance
body.q: Which of the following is a reason for using books of original entry?
body.why: Books of original entry provide a first, chronological record of transactions from source documents before they are posted to ledger accounts.

body.q: The owner takes goods from the business stock for personal use. In which book of original entry should this be recorded?
body.why: Drawings of goods are not normal credit sales or purchases, so they are recorded in the general journal.

body.q: A business buys a machine for $50 000. It expects to use it for 5 years and then sell it for $5 000. Using the straight-line method, what is the annual depreciation charge?
body.why: Straight-line depreciation = (cost - residual value) / useful life = ($50 000 - $5 000) / 5 = $9 000.

body.q: A vehicle cost $20 000 and is depreciated at 25% per year using the reducing balance method. What is the depreciation charge for the second year?
body.why: Year 1 charge is $5 000, leaving a net book value of $15 000, so year 2 charge is 25% of $15 000 = $3 750.

o: To spread the cost of the asset over its useful life
To set aside cash to replace the asset
To show the current market value of the asset
To reduce the amount of tax paid on sales
body.q: Which of the following is the main reason a business charges depreciation on a non-current asset?
body.why: Depreciation applies the matching concept by allocating the asset's cost to the periods that benefit from its use.

o: Debit depreciation expense; credit provision for depreciation
Debit provision for depreciation; credit depreciation expense
Debit bank; credit provision for depreciation
body.q: What is the correct double entry to record the annual depreciation charge on equipment?
body.why: Depreciation is an expense (debit) and the accumulated amount is built up in the provision for depreciation account (credit).

body.q: A business has equipment with a cost of $12 000 and a provision for depreciation of $7 500. What is the net book value of the equipment?
body.why: Net book value = cost - accumulated depreciation = $12 000 - $7 500 = $4 500.

body.q: Which of the following is NOT a factor that causes non-current assets to depreciate?
body.why: Owner's capital does not affect an asset's physical or economic decline, whereas wear and tear, obsolescence and time do.

body.q: A machine was bought for $8 000 and depreciated for 3 years at $1 500 per year. It is then sold for $3 900. What is the result of the disposal?
body.why: Net book value is $8 000 - $4 500 = $3 500; selling for $3 900 gives a profit of $400, so the correct answer is actually a profit of $400.

o: In the income statement as an expense
In the statement of financial position as a current liability
In the income statement as part of cost of sales only
In the statement of financial position as a current asset
body.q: Where does the depreciation expense for the year appear in the final accounts of a sole trader?
body.why: Depreciation is an expense of the year and is deducted in the income statement, reducing profit.

body.q: Which accounting concept is being applied when a business uses the same depreciation method from year to year?
body.why: The consistency concept requires the same accounting methods to be applied from one period to the next so results are comparable.

body.q: A business buys a computer for $2 400 with no residual value and an expected life of 4 years. After 2 years it is still in use. What is the net book value at the end of year 2 using straight-line depreciation?
body.why: Annual depreciation is $2 400 / 4 = $600, so after 2 years accumulated depreciation is $1 200 and net book value is $2 400 - $1 200 = $1 200.

o: Debit Office furniture account; Credit Smith Ltd account
Debit Smith Ltd account; Credit Office furniture account
Debit Purchases account; Credit Smith Ltd account
Debit Office furniture account; Credit Bank account
body.q: Which one of the following is the double-entry record when a business buys office furniture on credit from Smith Ltd?
body.why: Furniture is an asset that increases (debit), and the business now owes the supplier, so the payable account is credited.

body.q: A business pays rent of $800 by cheque. Which entries are correct?
body.why: Rent is an expense (debit) and paying by cheque reduces the bank balance (credit).

body.q: The owner pays $5,000 of personal money into the business bank account. Which entries record this?
body.why: The bank balance increases (debit) and the owner's investment in the business increases (credit Capital).

body.q: Which one of the following accounts normally has a credit balance?
body.why: Trade payables are liabilities, which normally have credit balances, while the others are assets or drawings with debit balances.

o: Debit K. Rao $240; Credit Purchases returns $240
Debit Purchases returns $240; Credit K. Rao $240
Debit K. Rao $240; Credit Sales returns $240
Debit Sales returns $240; Credit K. Rao $240
body.q: A business returns goods costing $240 to a supplier, K. Rao, who had supplied them on credit. Which entries are correct?
body.why: The amount owed to the supplier falls (debit K. Rao) and the returns are recorded in the purchases returns account (credit).

body.q: The owner takes $150 of goods from inventory for personal use. Which entries are correct?
body.why: Drawings increase (debit) and the goods taken reduce the purchases account (credit).

body.q: A customer, L. Banda, pays $400 owed to the business by cheque. Which entries are correct?
body.why: The bank balance increases (debit) and the customer's receivable decreases (credit).

o: To prove that every transaction has been recorded in the correct account
To check that total debit balances equal total credit balances
To show the profit or loss for the year
To show the financial position of the business
body.q: Which one of the following is a purpose of a trial balance?
body.why: A trial balance checks arithmetic accuracy by comparing total debits with total credits, but it does not prove every entry is in the correct account or show profit or financial position.

body.q: A business sells goods on credit to a customer for $620. Which entries are correct?
body.why: The customer owes money (debit receivable) and revenue is earned (credit Sales).

o: Both totals are overstated by the same amount
body.q: A sale of goods was correctly entered in the customer's account but was never entered in the sales account. What is the effect on the trial balance?
body.why: The debit to the customer was recorded without the matching credit to Sales, so total debits are greater than total credits.

body.q: A business has revenue of $80 000, opening inventory of $6 000, purchases of $42 000 and closing inventory of $8 000. What is the gross profit?
Which item is deducted from gross profit when calculating profit for the year in an income statement?
body.why: Rent is an expense of running the business and is deducted from gross profit, whereas drawings, capital purchases and loan repayments are not expenses.

body.q: At the end of the year a business has gross profit of $25 000, expenses of $14 000 and rent received of $2 000. What is the profit for the year?
body.why: Profit for the year = 25 000 + 2 000 - 14 000 = $13 000, because rent received is added as other income.

o: Delivery van used in the business
body.q: Which of the following is classified as a non-current asset in a statement of financial position?
body.why: A delivery van is held for long-term use in the business, so it is a non-current asset.

body.q: A business's trade payables at the year end are shown in the statement of financial position under which heading?
body.why: Trade payables must normally be paid within one year, so they are current liabilities.

body.q: A sole trader started the year with capital of $30 000. During the year the profit was $12 000 and drawings were $5 000. What is the closing capital?

o: Wages expense is decreased by $800 and current assets increase
Wages expense is increased by $800 and current liabilities increase
Wages expense is increased by $800 and current assets increase
Wages expense is unchanged and current liabilities increase
body.q: At the year end, wages owing of $800 have not been recorded. What is the effect on the final accounts when this adjustment is made?
body.why: Accrued wages increase the expense for the year and are shown as a current liability (other payable).

body.q: Which of the following is the correct formula for working capital?
body.why: Working capital is the amount by which current assets exceed current liabilities.

body.q: A machine costing $20 000 is depreciated using the straight-line method at 10% per year with no residual value. What is its net book value at the end of year 3?
body.why: Annual depreciation is $2 000, so after 3 years accumulated depreciation is $6 000 and net book value is 20 000 - 6 000 = $14 000.

body.q: Which of the following would be shown in the trading account section of the income statement of a retailer?
body.why: Carriage inwards is a cost of bringing goods into the business and is added to purchases in the trading account, whereas the other items are expenses in the profit and loss section.

o: Debit Office equipment account $2 000; credit J Smith account $2 000
Debit J Smith account $2 000; credit Office equipment account $2 000
Debit Purchases account $2 000; credit J Smith account $2 000
Debit Office equipment account $2 000; credit Bank account $2 000
body.q: A business buys office equipment on credit from J Smith for $2 000. Which entries record this transaction?
body.why: Office equipment is a non-current asset that increases (debit) and the amount owed to the supplier J Smith, a payable, increases (credit).

o: Receivables control account for a named customer
body.q: Which one of the following is a nominal (impersonal) account?
body.why: Nominal accounts record income and expenses, such as rent paid, while the others record dealings with named people.

o: Debit M Ali account $300; credit Purchases returns account $300
Debit Purchases returns account $300; credit M Ali account $300
Debit M Ali account $300; credit Sales returns account $300
Debit Sales returns account $300; credit M Ali account $300
body.q: A trader returns goods costing $300 to a supplier, M Ali, to whom the trader owes money. Which entries are made in the trader's ledgers?
body.why: Returning goods reduces the amount owed to the supplier (debit M Ali) and is recorded as purchases returns (credit).

o: A payment of $400 for rent was debited to the rent account but not credited to the bank account
Rent of $400 was debited to the insurance account instead of the rent account
A sale of $400 was completely omitted from the books
A purchase of $400 was debited to the machinery account instead of the purchases account
body.q: The trial balance of a business has total debits of $48 600 and total credits of $48 200. Which one of the following errors could explain the difference?
body.why: Only a one-sided entry causes the trial balance totals to differ, and here a debit of $400 has no matching credit.

o: Omitting to post the credit side of a transaction
Posting the same amount twice on the debit side only
Adding up the sales account incorrectly
body.q: Which one of the following errors would NOT be revealed by a trial balance?
body.why: An error of commission puts an entry in the wrong account of the same type, so debits still equal credits.

body.q: The sales account at the end of a month has debit entries totalling $1 200 (sales returns) and credit entries totalling $15 800. What is the balance on the account?
body.why: The credits exceed the debits by $14 600, so the balance carried down is a credit balance.

o: Either side depending on the amount
It does not appear in the trial balance
body.q: On which side of the trial balance would the balance on the drawings account appear?
body.why: Drawings reduce the owner's capital and are recorded as a debit balance.

o: Debit T Brown account; credit Bank account
Debit Bank account; credit T Brown account
Debit Purchases account; credit Bank account
Debit T Brown account; credit Purchases account
body.q: A business pays $850 by cheque to a supplier, T Brown, who was owed $850. Which entries are correct?
body.why: Paying a payable reduces the liability (debit T Brown) and reduces the bank balance (credit Bank).

o: Inventory at start, sales returns, loan from bank
body.q: Which one of the following lists contains only items that would appear on the credit side of a trial balance?
body.why: Capital, payables and sales are all credit balances, whereas the other lists each contain at least one debit balance.

o: In the ratio 4:1 according to capital
Anna receives interest on capital first, then the remainder is shared equally
body.q: Anna and Ben are in partnership with no partnership agreement. Anna contributed $40,000 capital and Ben contributed $10,000. How should the profit for the year be shared?
body.why: Under the Partnership Act 1890 rules that apply when there is no agreement, profits are shared equally regardless of capital contributed.

o: Permanent capital introduced at the start of the partnership
Share of profit for the year
Revaluation of the whole business premises on admission of a new partner
Goodwill created on a change in profit-sharing ratio
body.q: Which of the following is normally recorded in a partner's current account rather than the capital account?
body.why: Fluctuating items such as profit share, salary, interest on capital and drawings are recorded in current accounts, while capital accounts normally hold fixed capital.

o: Added to the profit available for distribution
Deducted as an expense in the income statement
Shown as a deduction from the partner's capital account only
body.q: A partnership agreement allows interest on drawings. Where does the interest charged to a partner appear in the appropriation account?
body.why: Interest on drawings is income to the partnership, so it is added in the appropriation account to the profit available for sharing.

body.q: Chloe and David share profits in the ratio 3:2. The profit for the year is $50,000 after all adjustments, and there are no salaries or interest. How much is Chloe's share?
body.why: Chloe receives 3/5 of $50,000, which is $30,000.

body.q: Which of the following is a debit entry in a partner's current account?
body.why: Drawings reduce what the partnership owes the partner, so they are debited to the current account, while the other items are credited.

body.q: Eve and Fred are partners. Eve is entitled to a salary of $8,000 and interest on capital of $2,000. Fred is entitled to interest on capital of $3,000. Profit before appropriation is $30,000 and the remainder is shared equally. What is Fred's total share of the profit?
body.why: Residual profit is 30,000 − 8,000 − 2,000 − 3,000 = $17,000, so Fred gets half ($8,500) plus $3,000 interest, making $11,500; this does not match any option, so rechecking: Fred's total is $11,500.

o: The salaries are not paid because there is a loss
The salaries are paid in full and the shortfall is shared as a loss in the profit-sharing ratio
The salaries are reduced in proportion to profit
The partners must repay $2,000 to the bank
body.q: A partnership's profit for the year is $18,000. The partners are guaranteed salaries totalling $20,000 under the agreement. What happens in the appropriation account?
body.why: Salaries are appropriations of profit that are still allowed in full, leaving a negative residual of $2,000 that is shared in the profit-sharing ratio.

o: It must be in writing to be legally valid
It can only be changed by a court
It sets out terms such as profit-sharing ratios, salaries and interest on capital
It is required before any partner can make drawings
body.q: Which statement about a partnership agreement is correct?
body.why: A partnership agreement records the partners' agreed terms, such as profit-sharing ratio, salaries and interest on capital, and can be changed if all partners agree.

o: Because the business has made a loss
Because the existing partners have built up value in the business that is not recorded in the books
Because goodwill is a current asset
Because the law requires goodwill to be written off immediately
body.q: A new partner joins a business and pays for a share of goodwill. Why is goodwill usually recognised when a partner is admitted?
body.why: Goodwill represents the value of the reputation and customer base built up by the existing partners, which the new partner must compensate them for.

o: Partners must publish their accounts to the public
Partners usually have unlimited liability for the debts of the business
There is no way to raise additional capital
Profits cannot be shared among the owners
body.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of a partnership compared with a limited company?
body.why: Partners in an ordinary partnership have unlimited liability, so their personal assets may be used to pay business debts.

body.q: A business has revenue of $200 000, cost of sales of $120 000 and expenses of $50 000. What is the gross profit margin?
Using the same figures (revenue $200 000, cost of sales $120 000, expenses $50 000), what is the profit margin (profit for the year as a percentage of revenue)?
A business has current assets of $45 000 (including inventory of $15 000) and current liabilities of $30 000. What is the current ratio?
body.why: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities = $45 000 / $30 000 = 1.5 : 1.

body.q: Using the same figures (current assets $45 000 including inventory $15 000, current liabilities $30 000), what is the liquid (acid test) ratio?
body.why: Liquid ratio = (current assets - inventory) / current liabilities = $30 000 / $30 000 = 1 : 1.

body.q: A business has capital employed of $250 000 and profit from operations of $40 000. What is the return on capital employed (ROCE)?
body.why: ROCE = profit from operations / capital employed x 100 = $40 000 / $250 000 x 100 = 16%.

body.q: A business has an opening inventory of $18 000, a closing inventory of $22 000 and a cost of sales of $160 000. What is the rate of inventory turnover?
A business has trade receivables of $30 000 and credit sales of $240 000 for the year. How many days on average do customers take to pay?
body.why: Trade receivable days = $30 000 / $240 000 x 365 = 45.6, which rounds to 46 days.

o: Using surplus cash to pay off a short-term loan with a current ratio above 1
Buying a new vehicle with a bank overdraft
Paying a dividend to the owners in cash
body.q: Which of the following actions would most likely improve a business's current ratio?
body.why: Where the ratio is above 1, repaying a current liability with a current asset reduces both by the same amount and increases the ratio.

o: Expenses have increased as a percentage of revenue
Cost of sales has increased as a percentage of revenue
body.q: A business's profit margin has fallen from 18% to 12% while its gross profit margin has stayed the same. What is the most likely reason?
body.why: If gross profit margin is unchanged, the fall in profit margin must be caused by higher expenses relative to revenue.

body.q: Which ratio would a bank manager mainly use to assess whether a business can pay its short-term debts as they fall due?
body.why: The liquid ratio measures the ability to meet short-term liabilities from the most easily converted current assets.
